Graciela Iturbide was born (on May 16 in Mexico City). Her father from Michoacán, her mother from Aguascalientes. The eldest daughter in a family of 13 siblings. Raised in a conservative family, amidst festivities and religious representations.
Married architect Manuel Rocha Díaz. They have three children: Manuel, Claudia, and Mauricio.

At the age of 27, she enrolled in the Centro Universitario de Estudios Cinematográficos of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México. She discovered photography in the courses of Manuel Álvarez Bravo, who invited her to work with him. Don Manuel was her great mentor: “Graciela, don't rush, there is time. Don't rush to exhibit, you have to work hard.”
After the death of her 6-year-old daughter, Claudia, she separated from her husband and devoted herself full-time to her artistic work.

She traveled to Panama to photograph General Omar Torrijos, one of Latin America's best-known revolutionary figures. Also traveled to Mexican communities such as Ocumicho, Espinazo, San Agustín Etla, and Cuetzalan, among others.
Graciela Iturbide's first exhibition with Colette Alvarez Urbajtel and Paulina Lavista: Three Mexican Women Photographers at the Jose Clemente Orozco Gallery in Mexico City.

The Ethnographic Archives of the National Indigenous Institute of Mexico commissioned her to photograph the indigenous peoples of Mexico, along with other Mexican photographers such as Pablo Ortiz Monasterio, Mariana Yampolsky, and Nacho López. For a month, she went to photograph the Seris, in the Sonora desert, in the north of Mexico, on the Arizona border. This photoreportage was published in 1981 as Los que viven en la Arena.

Graciela Iturbide was invited by Francisco Toledo to photograph the Zapotecs of Juchitán, Oaxaca. For more than ten years, Graciela lived with its inhabitants. Stimulated by the observation of their daily life, the artist was able to photograph the Zapotec women with complete complicity and trust. The first photographs were exhibited at the Casa de la Cultura in Juchitán in 1980. The final series was published in 1989.
She receives the W. Eugene Smith photojournalism grant for her work in Juchitán.
Winner of the Grand Prize of the Month of the Photo in Paris. That same year receives a Guggenheim Fellowship for her photographs of funeral processions and death rituals in Chalma.

She visited Huajuapan de León in Tehuacán, Puebla, to photograph the slaughter of the goats, work published in the book En el nombre del padre (In the name of the father) in 1993. This experience marked the beginning of a new experience in her photographic practice that was more oriented towards the symbolic and abstract.
That same year, Médecins Sans Frontières invited her to Madagascar to make a series of portraits of women suffering from AIDS.
Graciela Iturbide's first exhibition in the United States was organized at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.
She was awarded the prize of the International Photography Encounters of Arles in France.
Francisco Toledo invited her to take photographs at the Oaxaca Botanical Garden. It was the beginning of her series Naturata, published in 2004.
The Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Monterrey (MARCO) organized the first retrospective of her work.
She traveled for a month and a half in the southern United States with poet Roberto Tejada to photograph the landscapes of Louisiana and Texas.

In the same year, she made his first trip to India, where he photographed objects. In 1999 she returned to India and Bangladesh where she photographed transvestites, wrestlers, and prostitutes. Graciela made five trips to India, which led to the publication of No hay nadie in 2011.
Her work is presented in a major retrospective at the Philadelphia Museum of Art in Pennsylvania.

After Frida Kahlo died in 1954, Diego Rivera decided to close two bathrooms containing Frida's objects and documents. More than 50 years later, in 2006, they were reopened and for this occasion, the Frida Kahlo Museum invited Graciela Iturbide to make a photographic testimony.
Graciela traveled to Rome and Sardinia in Italy. She published the book “Mexico-Rome” which confronts photographs of objects taken in Mexico in 1974 and 2009 with those taken in Rome in 2007.
In Los Angeles California, Graciela exhibited an important retrospective at the J. Paul Getty Museum where series taken in Mexico and the United States were shown.
Graciela Iturbide received the Hasselblad Award given by the Swedish Erna and Victor Hasselblad Foundation to photographers who have done outstanding work.
Architect Mauricio Rocha designed Estudio Iturbide on Heliotropo Street in the Niño Jesús neighborhood of Coyoacán, Mexico City. A three-story building in the spirit of a small clay tower.
Exhibition at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston devoted to Graciela Iturbide's photographs dedicated to Mexican communities and rituals.
The Cartier Foundation showed in Paris the exhibition Heliotrope 37, the first major exhibition in France devoted to Graciela Iturbide's oeuvre as a whole, from 1970 to 2022.
She received the William Klein Award at the Academy of Fine Arts in Paris.
The Javier Marín Foundation presents at the Centro Cultural Fábrica de San Pedro in Uruapan, Michoacán.
She was awarded the Gold Medal of Fine Arts in Mexico and the rank of Officer in the Order of Arts and Letters of the French Republic.
